Q: Errno 61: Connection refused error when trying to connect to python server A:

though they work perfectly when I run them both from the same computer, my attempts to connect the client when running on another computer results in the following error …

In the client, you still have host = '127.0.0.1' (i. e. localhost), but if you want to connect to a server on another computer, you have to set host to that computer's address. And in the server, you should change host = '127.0.0.1' to host = '0.0.0.0'.

Q: Custom Action, Unable to build custom action because the project output group does not have a key file A:

Within your installation project, you need to identify a key file in the Project Output group that you have referenced.

To resolve the issue, right-click on the appropriate project output that you have added to the installation program, expand the KeyOutput node, and click in the (Files) box and click the ... button.

If there is nothing in there, then you should probably remove that output from your installer.

Q: Why do aggregation functions work without Group By? A:

Adding more to above explanation: Try this SQL code without group by clause:
=> Select Employee_ID, max(salary) from Employee
It hits error as Employee_id returns multiple values but max(salary) will return one max value for entire result set. It doesn't know how to pivot the result. In such cases, we need group by clause.
We can modify this query like this:
=> Select Employee_ID, max(salary) from employees group by Employee_ID
Now, above code will run successfully

Q: the pointer existential crisis dielma: If pointer stores memory address then how are memory addresses of a pointers stored? A:

You appear to be under the impression that at run-time, the address of every variable must be explicitly stored in memory somewhere, so that every variable must have its own pointer somewhere in memory. And you appear to be under the impression that each of these pointers must also have its address stored explicitly in memory somewhere, which would mean that infinite levels of indirection (and therefore infinite amounts of memory) would be required for a program to have a single variable.

However, this is not the case. It is not necessary to store the addresses of all variables explicitly in memory at run-time. Rather, in order to access all local variables of a function, only the address of the stack frame of the function has to be stored at run-time.

This stack frame usually contains all local variables of a function, so you don't need a separate pointer for each variable. You only need a single pointer to the stack frame of the function, in order to access all local variables of the function.

You don't need the address of this stack frame pointer. This pointer probably does not even have a memory address, because it likely resides inside a CPU register (for example inside the RBP register when using an x86-64 CPU).

The code that the compiler generates will likely contain offsets from the start of the stack frame, which specify the position of the local variable inside the stack frame which the code wants to access.

Q: Prettier plugin not resolved when using GitHub package with pnpm, but works with npm A:

Unfortunately, @Rafael's answer didn't work for me. From what I understand, packageExtensions is for dependency resolution, whereas prettier searches for the plugin binaries, which are simply unavailable in the non-flat dependency structure.

This worked for me:

import { createRequire } from "node:module";
const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);

/**
 * @see https://prettier.io/docs/configuration
 * @type {import("prettier").Config}
 */
module.exports = {
  tabWidth: 4,
  semi: false,
  singleQuote: true,
  importOrder: [
    '^react|^react-dom',
    '<THIRD_PARTY_MODULES>',
    '^@core/(.*)$',
    '^@server/(.*)$',
    '^@ui/(.*)$',
    '^[./]',
    '<TYPES>',
  ],
  importOrderSortSpecifiers: true,
  importOrderMergeDuplicateImports: true,
  plugins: [require.resolve('@ianvs/prettier-plugin-sort-imports')],
}

this forces prettier to see the absolute path to the resolved module, and leaves out the guesswork which happens fine for npm but not for pnpm.
